title: Quarks, hadrons and leptons
prior_knowledge_summary: A proton and neutron are nucleons in the nucleus, while electrons occupy the space around it.
Nucleon number and charge are conserved in nuclear processes.
An antiparticle has the same mass but opposite charge to its corresponding particle.
Beta-minus decay emits an electron and electron antineutrino, while beta-plus decay emits a positron and electron neutrino.
new_learning: A quark is fundamental, and the six flavours are up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom.
Up, charm and top quarks have charge +2/3 e; down, strange and bottom quarks have charge -1/3 e; antiquark charges have the opposite signs.
Protons are uud and neutrons are udd; both are baryons and are not fundamental.
A baryon contains three quarks, while a meson contains one quark and one antiquark.
At quark level beta-minus changes d to u and beta-plus changes u to d.
Electrons and neutrinos are fundamental particles called leptons.

blocks.title: What is inside a proton?
content: A proton looks like one particle in a decay equation. But suppose a probe could look deeper. Would it find a smaller structure?

The surprising answer is yes. A proton is built from quarks, while an electron is not known to contain smaller particles. Today we need a map that separates building blocks from particles built out of them.

figure.purpose: Create the central puzzle by contrasting a visibly composite proton with an indivisible electron.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch. Show a proton circle opening to reveal three small coloured quark marks, beside an electron drawn as one simple dot with a question mark. Use sparse labels and do not yet label the particle families.
figure.alt_text: A proton opens to reveal three smaller constituents while an electron remains a single dot.

blocks.title: Fundamental means no smaller constituents

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a particle that cannot be divided into smaller particles

content: A fundamental particle is a particle that cannot be divided into smaller particles.
Quarks are fundamental particles. The six flavours are up, down, strange, charm, top and bottom. Flavour here means type. It does not mean taste.
Electrons and neutrinos are also fundamental. They belong to a family called leptons. A proton and a neutron are different: each contains quarks, so neither is fundamental.

misconception.claim: A very small particle must be fundamental.
misconception.why_it_feels_right: Small objects can look structureless when our probe cannot resolve their parts.
misconception.where_it_fails: Fundamental describes whether there are smaller constituents, not merely the object's size.
misconception.resolution: Ask whether the particle is built from smaller particles. Protons and neutrons are made from quarks, while quarks, electrons and neutrinos are treated as fundamental here.

figure.purpose: Separate fundamental particles from composite particles using constituent structure.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper hand-drawn sorting board. Left column: quark, electron and neutrino as single marks under fundamental. Right column: proton and neutron as clusters of three quark marks under composite. Use a small magnifying-glass motif and generous white space.
figure.alt_text: Quarks, electrons and neutrinos are sorted as fundamental, while protons and neutrons are shown as three-quark composites.

blocks.title: Two charge groups make the quark table manageable
content: The six names are easier to learn in two charge groups. Up, charm and top each have charge +2/3 e. Down, strange and bottom each have charge -1/3 e.
An antiquark has the opposite charge to its quark. So an antiup has charge -2/3 e, while an antidown has charge +1/3 e. The bar over a symbol means anti.

Think of charge as a ledger. Add every constituent charge, including its sign. For a quark-antiquark pair u and antidown, the total is +2/3 e + 1/3 e = +e. The reverse check is that the two signed fractions must add to the stated whole charge.

figure.purpose: Teach all six quark charges and the sign reversal for antiquarks as two memorable families.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper charge table in two coloured rows. Row one groups u, c, t at +2/3 e and their antiquarks at -2/3 e. Row two groups d, s, b at -1/3 e and their antiquarks at +1/3 e. Use hand-drawn fraction bars and short opposite-sign arrows.
figure.alt_text: The six quark flavours are grouped by charge, with each antiquark shown carrying the opposite charge.

blocks.title: Build a proton and a neutron from signed charges
content: A proton contains uud. Add its charges: +2/3 e + 2/3 e - 1/3 e = +3/3 e = +e. This agrees with the proton charge.
A neutron contains udd. Add its charges: +2/3 e - 1/3 e - 1/3 e = 0. This agrees with the neutron charge.
The charge calculation is an independent check on the remembered compositions. It also shows why a neutron can have zero total charge even though its quarks carry charge.

figure.purpose: Make proton and neutron composition and signed charge addition visible in parallel.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper split worked layout. Left: proton with u, u, d tokens and a vertical charge sum ending +e. Right: neutron with u, d, d tokens and a sum ending 0. Keep arithmetic visible and hand written.
figure.alt_text: Parallel quark-charge sums show uud has charge plus e and udd has zero charge.

blocks.title: Hadrons come in two structures
content: A particle made from quarks is a hadron. A baryon consists of three quarks. Protons and neutrons are baryons.
A meson consists of one quark and one antiquark. The quickest classification method is to count the constituents and notice whether an anti symbol is present.

A common trap is to call every three-constituent combination a baryon. At this level a baryon is three quarks, while a meson is one quark plus one antiquark. An electron or neutrino is neither: each is a lepton.

figure.purpose: Contrast baryon, meson and lepton structures without relying only on names.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison card with three panels: baryon as q+q+q, meson as q+antiquark, and lepton as one indivisible dot. Include proton uud and a generic meson as examples, but no practice answers.
figure.alt_text: A baryon has three quarks, a meson has a quark-antiquark pair, and a lepton is shown as fundamental.

blocks.title: Beta decay changes one quark
content: Earlier, beta-minus decay changed a neutron into a proton. Now compare the internal structures: neutron udd becomes proton uud. Only one symbol changes, so one down quark changes into an up quark: d to u.
For beta-plus decay the direction reverses. Proton uud becomes neutron udd, so one up quark changes into a down quark: u to d.

Check beta-minus by charge. The changing quark charge rises from -1/3 e to +2/3 e, an increase of +e. The emitted electron carries -e, so charge still balances when the neutral antineutrino is included. For beta-plus, the quark change is -e and the emitted positron is +e.

figure.purpose: Connect familiar nucleon-level beta decay to the single quark-flavour change and its charge check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper two-row sequence. Top: beta-minus, udd arrow uud with the changing d and u highlighted, plus electron and antineutrino leaving. Bottom: beta-plus, uud arrow udd with u and d highlighted, plus positron and neutrino leaving. Add compact signed charge ledgers.
figure.alt_text: Beta-minus changes one down quark to up, while beta-plus changes one up quark to down, with emitted leptons shown.

blocks.title: A three-question particle map
content: First ask: can the particle be divided into smaller particles? If no, it may be a quark or lepton. Electrons and neutrinos are leptons.
If it contains quarks, ask how many and whether one is an antiquark. Three quarks means baryon. One quark and one antiquark means meson.
Finally, add signed quark charges to check the identity. For beta decay, compare the nucleon compositions before and after and identify the one changed quark.

figure.purpose: Provide a compact decision route for particle classification, charge checking and beta-decay changes.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper hand-drawn flow map. Begin with smaller constituents, branch to fundamental or hadron, then branch hadron to three quarks or quark-antiquark. Finish with small charge-check and before-after beta-change boxes.
figure.alt_text: A decision map classifies fundamental particles, baryons and mesons, then checks charge and beta-decay quark changes.
